categories.name: Payer mix strategy
categories.summary: Which payers the practice's revenue comes from, what each pays per visit, how fast and how reliably. Payer mix is partly a choice: which plans to join, which to leave, and which patients and sites to pursue.
good_looks_like: Revenue, visits and payment per visit are reported by payer class every quarter.
The practice knows its three best and three worst payers by net payment per visit and by denial rate.
Dependence on any one payer is known and planned for.
Decisions to join or leave a plan are made from numbers.
failure_modes: The practice joins every plan offered and never checks which ones pay less than the cost of the visit.
One payer provides most of the revenue and its yearly rate change is never modeled.
A plan's low rate is tolerated because nobody added up its denials and delays too.
Payer mix shifts toward slower, lower-paying plans without anyone noticing.
key_questions: What share of revenue comes from each payer class?
What do we collect per visit from each payer, after denials?
Which plan would we drop if we could, and what would it cost us?
How has the mix changed in two years?

actions.detail: Charges, payments, visits, payment per visit, denial rate and days to pay.

actions.action: Rank payers by what each really pays per visit
actions.detail: Payment per visit after denials and write-offs, beside the staff time each payer takes.

actions.action: Model the largest payer's rate change
actions.detail: Each November for Medicare, when the final fee schedule rule comes out, and at each contract renewal for plans.

actions.action: Decide yearly on each small plan
actions.detail: Keep, renegotiate or leave, with the access consequences for patients and sites.

categories.applies_when: Every practice, and most of all practices serving older adults, which live on Medicare and Medicare Advantage and mostly choose which plans to contract with. For facility-based practices the mix comes with the buildings served: residents arrive with their coverage, so decide by facility and plan.

vendor_refs.note: Adds tracking each payer's share of visits beside its share of revenue. Its 25% single-payer alarm and its pay bands by payer class cite no source.
Puts 55% to 75% of a geriatric panel in Medicare Advantage with no source. Wrongly says those plans need not follow Medicare's coverage rules.

categories.evidence_note: Management practice. Denial rates by payer type are measured in peer-reviewed studies: Medicare Advantage 17% of first claims (2019), Medicaid fee-for-service 17.8 points above Medicare (2013 to 2015). No benchmark for an ideal mix exists.

metrics.name: Share of revenue from the largest payer
metrics.definition: Payments from the single largest payer, with its patients' cost sharing, as a share of all payments received.
metrics.formula: Largest payer's payments / total payments from all payers and patients
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. It measures dependence. AMA survey, 2016 data: physicians' patients averaged 43% commercial, 29% Medicare and 17% Medicaid. More than half (55%) of eligible Medicare beneficiaries were in Medicare Advantage in 2026 (KFF). Above half on one payer, model its rate changes yearly.
metrics.data_hint: Payments by payer from the billing system.
metrics.vendor_claim: The purchased library calls any payer above 25% of net revenue a concentration risk.
metrics.vendor_verdict: Unverifiable. No source is given. A practice serving older adults passes 25% on Medicare by design, so the alarm would never clear.

metrics.name: Net revenue per visit by payer
metrics.definition: Payments received from a payer, including its patients' cost sharing collected, divided by visits billed to that payer.
metrics.formula: Payments for the payer's patients / visits billed to that payer
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found, because the figure depends on the mix of codes billed. Compare with your own trend. Compare payers with each other and with Medicare's allowed amount for the same codes.

categories.name: Contract inventory and terms
categories.summary: Holding a signed copy of every payer agreement and its current fee schedule, and knowing the terms that cost money when missed: filing and appeal deadlines, amendment rules, renewal and termination dates.
good_looks_like: One folder holds every payer contract, amendment and fee schedule.
A register lists each contract's effective date, renewal date, notice period, filing limit and appeal deadline.
Fee schedules are loaded where payments can be checked against them.
Payer notices of amendment are read and answered before their deadline.
Staff know the notice rules. In Florida, a health maintenance organization owes 30 days' written notice of payment schedule changes and 60 days' notice before ending a contract without cause.
failure_modes: The practice cannot find its contract, so it cannot dispute an underpayment in time. In Florida the limit is 12 months after the payment for state-regulated plans.
A plan changes rates by a mailed or posted notice that takes effect unless the practice objects within the contract's window, and nobody reads it.
A contract renews automatically for years at an old rate.
Filing limits differ by payer (12 months for Original Medicare, 6 months for Florida-regulated plans, contract terms for Medicare Advantage) and staff apply one rule to all.
key_questions: Do we hold a signed contract and current fee schedule for every plan we bill?
What is each plan's filing limit and appeal deadline?
Which contracts renew or can be reopened in the next 12 months?
Who reads payer notices, and how fast?

actions.action: Collect every contract and fee schedule
actions.detail: Request missing copies from each plan's provider relations or network office.
Dates, notice periods, filing and appeal limits, amendment clause, contact, and plan type (state-regulated, employer self-funded, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid), since different laws apply to each.

actions.action: Load fee schedules into the billing system
actions.detail: So that each payment can be compared with the expected amount.
Record the date received and the reply deadline for every amendment or policy notice, including those posted on plan websites. Object in writing while the window is open.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that contracts with health plans. Medicare fee-for-service has no negotiated contract, but its fee schedule should be loaded the same way.

vendor_refs.note: Adds a clause reading list and a contract register. Its typical state payment deadline, 30 to 45 days, is not Florida's 20. Omits that self-funded plans escape state law.
Adds a control for amendment notices: one owner, a dated log, calendared reply dates. Calls silent acceptance simply legal and cites no state or Medicare Advantage notice rule.

categories.evidence_note: Regulation and statute. Medicare Advantage plans must give written notice of material rule changes and 60 days' notice before ending a contract without cause (42 CFR 422.202). Florida examples: sections 627.6131, 641.3155 and 641.315. State laws usually do not reach employer self-funded plans.

metrics.name: Payers with a signed contract and current fee schedule on file
metrics.definition: Share of contracted payers for which the practice holds the signed agreement and the fee schedule now in force.
metrics.formula: Payers with contract and current fee schedule on file / contracted payers
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.
metrics.data_hint: The contract register, checked against the list of payers billed in the last 12 months.

categories.name: Rate analysis and negotiation
categories.summary: Comparing what each plan pays with Medicare and with other plans for the practice's own most-used codes, and asking for better terms where the practice has something the plan needs.
good_looks_like: Each plan's rates for the practice's top codes are expressed as a percentage of Medicare.
The practice knows what it offers each plan: access, quality results, coverage of sites the plan must serve.
Requests are made in writing, with data, well before renewal.
Terms other than rates are negotiated too: filing limits, appeal rights, amendment notice.
failure_modes: A plan pays below Medicare and nobody has calculated it.
The practice asks for more with no data and accepts the first refusal.
A rate increase is won and never loaded, so underpayments go unnoticed.
Charges are set below a plan's allowed amount, so the practice caps its own payment.
key_questions: For our top 15 codes, what does each plan pay as a percent of Medicare?
Which plan is furthest below the others?
What do we offer that a plan needs?
Are our charges above every plan's allowed amount?

actions.detail: Top 15 codes by revenue, each plan's allowed amount, and Medicare's for the same locality.
Volume, access, quality and cost results, and the specific rates requested.

actions.action: Ask in writing 120 days before renewal
actions.detail: And follow up on a schedule.
Check the first month of remittances after any change.

categories.applies_when: Practices with commercial, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid managed care contracts. Small practices have little bargaining power on rates but can often win better non-rate terms, and gain power where a plan needs coverage of specific sites or populations.
categories.evidence_note: Method is professional practice. No reliable public benchmark for plan rates relative to Medicare was found, since contract rates are confidential.

metrics.name: Contracted rates as a percent of Medicare, by payer
metrics.definition: For the practice's main codes, each plan's allowed amount divided by Medicare's allowed amount for the same code and locality.
metrics.formula: Plan allowed amount / Medicare allowed amount, weighted by the practice's code volume
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Compare plans with each other. Any plan below 100% deserves a decision.
metrics.data_hint: Fee schedules or allowed amounts on remittances, against the Medicare fee schedule lookup.

categories.name: Credentialing and enrollment
categories.summary: Getting each clinician enrolled with Medicare, Medicaid and every plan, at every location, before they see patients, and keeping those enrollments current. A claim is payable only if the clinician was enrolled on the date of service.
good_looks_like: A tracker lists every clinician, payer and location with status, effective date and next revalidation or recredentialing date.
Applications are filed the day a clinician's offer is signed.
Revalidation and recredentialing requests are answered well before the deadline.
Changes of address, ownership or clinicians are reported within the required time.
failure_modes: A clinician sees patients for months before enrollment is effective, and the visits cannot be billed.
A recredentialing letter goes to an old address and the plan terminates the practice.
A new location is never added to the enrollment record.
The clinician's national provider record lists the wrong specialty or address.
key_questions: Is every clinician enrolled and current with every payer we bill?
When is each next revalidation or recredentialing due?
How many claims were denied last quarter for enrollment reasons?
Are our national provider records and practice locations up to date?

actions.detail: Clinician, payer, location, status, effective date, next due date, last contact.

actions.action: File at offer acceptance and follow up weekly
actions.detail: Medicare's effective date depends on the filing date, with only a short look-back.
Including the profile used by health plans, which must be re-attested regularly.
Medicare requires reports of ownership and location changes within 30 days and most other changes within 90.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that bills insurers. Each clinician needs separate enrollment with Medicare, with Medicaid where dual-eligible patients are seen, and with each plan.
categories.evidence_note: Medicare's rules are federal regulation, and its contractor publishes processing times. Plan credentialing timelines are set by each plan and are not published.

metrics.name: Clinician and payer pairs that are active and current
metrics.definition: Share of clinician-payer-location combinations the practice bills that are enrolled, effective and not past a revalidation date.
metrics.formula: Active and current enrollments / enrollments the practice needs
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.

metrics.name: Days from application to billable
metrics.definition: Calendar days from submitting a complete enrollment application to the date the clinician can be paid by that payer.
metrics.formula: Effective or approval date - complete application date, by payer
metrics.benchmark_note: First Coast, Medicare's contractor in Florida: 95% of clean online applications processed in 15 days and all within 50. Health plans publish no figures and often take longer.

metrics.name: Denials for enrollment or credentialing
metrics.definition: Share of claims denied because the rendering or billing clinician was not enrolled or eligible with the payer on the date of service.
metrics.formula: Claims denied for provider enrollment reasons / claims adjudicated
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. These are fully preventable, so the target is zero.
metrics.data_hint: Remittance reason codes for provider not eligible or not enrolled.

categories.name: Medicare fee-for-service rules and the annual fee schedule
categories.summary: How Original Medicare pays: a national fee schedule set each year, adjusted by locality and by whether the service was given in a facility. Each November's final rule changes what the practice will be paid from January.
good_looks_like: Someone reads the summary of the final rule each November and lists what changes for the practice's codes.
The top codes are repriced at next year's rates before the year starts.
The practice knows whether each service is paid at the facility or non-facility rate, and why.
Participation status is a deliberate choice.
failure_modes: The conversion factor falls and the practice learns it from its January deposits.
A place-of-service error pays the wrong rate for years.
A code is deleted or replaced on January 1 and claims are rejected for weeks.
Budgeting assumes last year's rates.
key_questions: What does next year's final rule do to our top 15 codes?
Which of our services are paid at the facility rate?
Have deleted, new or revised codes been loaded for January?
Are we a participating provider, and do we know what that means?

actions.action: Read the final rule summary each November
actions.detail: CMS publishes a fact sheet. Note the conversion factor and any policy touching the practice's services.
Next year's rate by code and place of service, times this year's volume.
New, deleted and revised codes and any modifier changes.

actions.action: Check place of service on a sample
actions.detail: Facility and non-facility rates differ, sometimes by a third.

categories.applies_when: Every practice that bills Original Medicare. The effect of each year's rule depends on the practice's code mix and settings: recent rules have treated services in facility settings differently from office services.
categories.evidence_note: The fee schedule and its yearly changes are federal rulemaking. The 2026 conversion factors are $33.40 and $33.57. The 2027 rule sets $32.63 and $32.95, a 2.31% cut.

metrics.name: Estimated revenue effect of the coming year's Medicare fee schedule
metrics.definition: Change in yearly Medicare revenue expected from the next fee schedule, holding volume and code mix constant.
metrics.formula: Sum over codes of (next year's rate - this year's rate) x this year's volume
metrics.benchmark_note: For 2027 the conversion factor falls 2.31% for most clinicians (CMS final rule, November 2026). Code-level and setting-level changes can add to or offset that.
metrics.data_hint: Volume by code and place of service from the billing system, with the Medicare fee schedule lookup for both years.

categories.name: Medicare Advantage operations
categories.summary: Working with private Medicare plans: confirming network status, meeting each plan's authorization and referral rules, tracking slower and less certain payment, and disputing denials. Each plan is a separate set of rules.
good_looks_like: A one-page sheet per plan lists network status, authorization and referral rules, filing limit, dispute process and contacts.
Enrollment in a plan is confirmed monthly for continuing patients.
Denials are tracked by plan and disputed through the contract's process.
The practice knows what happens to billing when a plan member elects hospice.
failure_modes: Staff assume a plan follows Original Medicare's rules and are surprised by denials.
A patient switches plans and the practice bills the old one for months.
Denials are written off, although most disputed denials are overturned.
Claims for a plan member on hospice keep going to the plan.
key_questions: For each plan, are we in network, and what needs authorization or a referral?
What is each plan's denial rate and average days to pay?
How many denials did we dispute last quarter, and how many did we win?
Do we re-check plan enrollment every month?

actions.action: Write a one-page sheet per plan
actions.detail: Network status, product types, authorization and referral rules, filing and dispute deadlines, contacts.

actions.action: Track denials and days to pay by plan
actions.detail: Monthly, beside Original Medicare for comparison.
Use the contract's dispute process and cite Medicare coverage rules, which plans must follow.
From the election date Original Medicare pays, and claims need the hospice modifiers.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with Medicare-age patients. Residents of nursing facilities and people with both Medicare and Medicaid can change plans during the year, so enrollment has to be re-checked monthly.
categories.evidence_note: Denial and overturn rates are from a peer-reviewed study of 2019 claims and from KFF's analysis of plan data. Federal rules, not state prompt-payment laws, govern these plans.

metrics.name: Medicare Advantage initial denial rate
metrics.definition: Share of claims to Medicare Advantage plans that are denied on first adjudication, reported by plan.
metrics.formula: Medicare Advantage claims denied on first adjudication / Medicare Advantage claims adjudicated
metrics.benchmark_note: Health Affairs, 2025, using 2019 claims: plans denied 17% of initial claims and 57% of denials were later overturned. Set targets by plan, not as one blended figure.

metrics.name: Share of revenue from Medicare Advantage
metrics.definition: Payments from Medicare Advantage plans as a share of total payments.
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. A rising share means more of the practice's revenue depends on contracts, authorization rules and dispute work.

categories.name: Medicaid and dual-eligible rules
categories.summary: The rules for patients who have Medicaid, alone or alongside Medicare. They decide whether any secondary payment arrives, whether the patient may be billed, and which managed care plan is responsible.
good_looks_like: Every clinician who sees dual-eligible patients is enrolled with the state Medicaid program.
Staff know that Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries may not be billed for Medicare cost sharing.
Coinsurance that Medicaid will not pay is posted as a contractual adjustment, not left as a balance.
The practice knows each Medicaid managed care plan's filing limit and payment method.
failure_modes: A clinician is not enrolled with Medicaid, so crossover claims are rejected and nothing is paid.
Patients protected by federal law receive statements for coinsurance.
Uncollectible dual-eligible balances inflate receivables for years.
A Medicaid plan's short filing limit is missed.
key_questions: Are all our clinicians enrolled with Medicaid?
What share of our Medicare patients also have Medicaid?
How much secondary payment do we actually receive on those patients?
Are protected patients flagged so they never get a statement?

actions.detail: And calendar its revalidation.
Identify Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries from the eligibility answer and suppress statements.
Use a specific adjustment code so it can be reported separately.
Filing limit, crossover handling and whether it pays electronically.

categories.applies_when: Practices serving low-income older or disabled patients, including most nursing facility practices. State rules differ. In Florida, Medicaid pays nothing on Medicare coinsurance when Medicare's payment already meets Medicaid's own rate.
categories.evidence_note: The ban on billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries is federal law. State payment rules on crossover claims vary, and most states limit them in a similar way.

metrics.name: Share of patients who are dual eligible
metrics.definition: Patients with both Medicare and Medicaid as a share of the practice's Medicare patients.
metrics.benchmark_note: Not a target. CMS publishes each clinician's share for fee-for-service patients. A high share means much coinsurance is uncollectible by law.
metrics.data_hint: Eligibility data, or the CMS public file by clinician.

metrics.name: Secondary payment received on dual-eligible coinsurance
metrics.definition: Payments received from Medicaid on Medicare coinsurance and deductibles, as a share of the amounts crossed over.
metrics.formula: Medicaid crossover payments / Medicare cost sharing crossed over to Medicaid
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Expect a low figure in states with lesser-of payment rules. Its use is to confirm crossovers are being processed at all.
metrics.data_hint: Secondary remittances from Medicaid against Medicare cost sharing.

categories.name: Payment policy monitoring
categories.summary: Watching for rule changes that alter what gets paid: Medicare's yearly rule, the regional contractor's coverage policies and review topics, plan policy bulletins and yearly code updates. Each change should become a written rule in the billing process.
good_looks_like: One person is responsible for reading payer and contractor updates on a schedule.
Each relevant change is turned into a dated entry in the practice's billing rules.
The contractor's list of services under targeted review is checked against what the practice bills.
Yearly code changes are loaded before January.
failure_modes: The practice learns of a policy change from a wave of denials.
A contractor announces a review of a service the practice bills heavily and nobody sees it.
A rule is learned once and forgotten when staff change.
Plan bulletins go to an unread mailbox.
key_questions: Who reads Medicare contractor and plan updates, and how often?
Is any service we bill on the contractor's active review list?
Where are our billing rules written down, with dates?
How did we find out about the last policy change that affected us?

actions.detail: Contractor news, coverage policy changes, the review topic list and each plan's bulletins.
One entry per rule, with its source and the date it took effect.

actions.action: Check billed services against review topics
actions.detail: If a high-volume service is listed, audit it before the contractor does.

actions.action: Subscribe to the contractor's and plans' notices
actions.detail: Sent to a mailbox someone reads.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Those using automated billing should treat each policy change as a change to the automation's rules, reviewed before release.
categories.evidence_note: Federal compliance guidance expects practices to keep current with payer rules. Contractors publish their review topics, so monitoring them is straightforward.

metrics.name: Payer policy review cadence
metrics.definition: How often a named person reviews Medicare contractor and plan policy updates and records the result.
metrics.formula: Count of documented policy reviews in the last 12 months
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Monthly is a reasonable standard, with a yearly read of the Medicare fee schedule rule.

categories.name: Veterans, military, commercial and out-of-network payers
categories.summary: The smaller payers, each with its own gatekeeping: Veterans Affairs community care, the military health plan, workers' compensation, small commercial plans, and patients seen out of network or with no insurance.
good_looks_like: For each small payer the practice has decided to participate properly or not at all.
Veterans Affairs community care visits have an authorization on file before the service.
Out-of-network and self-pay patients get the notices the law requires.
Write-offs for unenrolled payers are counted, so the cost of not enrolling is known.
failure_modes: A clinician sees patients from a payer that has never credentialed them, and every claim is written off.
Veterans' visits are billed with no authorization number.
An out-of-network bill breaks surprise-billing rules.
Small-plan claims are abandoned because each needs a phone call.
key_questions: Which payers do we bill without being enrolled or contracted?
How much did we write off last year for those payers?
Do Veterans Affairs community care visits always have an authorization first?
Do we ever bill patients out of network, and do we give the required notices?

actions.action: List every payer billed without enrollment
actions.detail: With last year's charges and write-offs for each.

actions.action: Decide for each: enroll or stop
actions.detail: Enroll where volume justifies it. Otherwise refer or schedule those patients differently.

actions.action: Require authorization for veterans' community care
actions.detail: Record the authorization number before the visit.

actions.action: Give required notices to self-pay patients
actions.detail: A good-faith estimate for scheduled services.

categories.applies_when: Practices with a scattering of patients outside their main payers. Federal surprise-billing rules mainly concern out-of-network care at hospitals and surgery centers for commercially insured patients, so they touch facility-visit practices only at the edges.
categories.evidence_note: Rules differ by payer and are set by statute, regulation and program manuals. This area is guidance on managing the long tail, with no benchmark.

metrics.name: Share of charges billed out of network
metrics.definition: Charges billed to payers with which the practice or the rendering clinician has no enrollment or contract, as a share of total charges.
metrics.formula: Charges to non-enrolled or non-contracted payers / total charges
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. Read it with the write-offs on those charges, which show what non-enrollment costs.
metrics.data_hint: Charges by payer against the enrollment tracker.
